paper_metadata.title: BQ-Bank: A Quantum Software for Finance and Banking

summary: BQ-Bank presents three gate-based quantum finance modules: option pricing via quantum amplitude estimation, VaR estimation via quantum amplitude estimation, and portfolio optimization via QAOA. The paper reports qualitative quadratic speedups for the first two modules and a hybrid QAOA workflow for the third, but it does not provide concrete device-level resource counts or a practical quantum advantage demonstration; the only explicit problem sizes mentioned are a two-asset VaR example over 30 holding days and a portfolio-optimization toy instance.

experiments.description: Quantum amplitude estimation-based option pricing for European-style call/put options, compared against Black-Scholes and classical Monte Carlo.

algorithm.ansatz: parameterized quantum circuits for state preparation

hyperparameters.n: number of qubits for discretized price register
hyperparameters.c: small rotation constant in amplitude encoding

problem_formulation.encoding_details: Underlying asset price distribution discretized into 2^n basis states; an extra qubit marks whether payoff is in the money; an ancillary qubit is rotated according to encoded payoff.
problem_formulation.objective_function: Estimate option price e^{-rT} E[f(S)] where f(S)=max(0,S-K) for call and analogous put payoff.
problem_formulation.constraints_handling: No explicit constraints; payoff encoded into amplitudes and estimated via QAE.

problem_instance.description: European-style option pricing under the Black-Scholes model.

dataset_specification.description: Underlying asset price distribution generated from a stochastic process / Black-Scholes assumptions.

problem_instance.data_preprocessing_details: Price distribution p(S_T) is sampled and discretized into pi; encoded into amplitudes of an n-qubit state.
problem_instance.evaluation_methodology: Compared quantum algorithm output with Black-Scholes standard value and classical Monte Carlo; results shown for a single example in figures.

implementation_details.classical_preprocessing: Discretize the terminal price distribution; encode payoff into a controlled rotation.
implementation_details.classical_postprocessing: Estimate expected payoff from measured ancilla probability and discount by e^{-rT}.

speedup_claims.conditions: QAE-based option pricing; precision scaling in the paper is O(M^-1) versus Monte Carlo O(M^-1/2)
speedup_claims.caveats: The paper states the asymptotic advantage qualitatively; no runtime benchmark or resource count is reported.

speedup_claims.factor: closer to Black-Scholes than classical Monte Carlo
speedup_claims.conditions: single example shown in figures for option pricing and expected option revenues
speedup_claims.caveats: No error bars, number of runs, or statistical significance reported.

complexity_analysis.quantum_complexity: quadratic speedup over classical Monte Carlo (as stated qualitatively via QAE)
complexity_analysis.classical_complexity: Monte Carlo O(M^{-1/2}) error scaling; QAE gives O(M^{-1}) precision in the paper's notation

advantage_assessment.resources_for_advantage: An n-qubit price register plus one payoff qubit and one ancilla are described; no concrete qubit count, depth, or shot budget is reported.
limiting_factors: Only a qualitative quadratic speedup over Monte Carlo is claimed
No concrete hardware scale or runtime data are reported
State preparation and amplitude estimation require nontrivial data loading
Comparison is against classical Monte Carlo and Black-Scholes on a toy example

notes: Hardware type inferred as real_qpu_superconducting because the paper states the software can run on a real quantum computer such as a superconducting system, but no specific device is named.

The paper does not give an explicit total qubit count for the option-pricing circuit; only an n-qubit price register plus one extra qubit and one ancillary qubit are described, so num_qubits is left null/inferred only at the register level.
The paper states the quantum option-pricing result is closer to Black-Scholes than classical Monte Carlo in the shown example, but provides no rigorous practical advantage benchmark.

experiments.description: Quantum amplitude estimation-based Value at Risk (VaR) estimation, compared with H-VaR, P-VaR, and Monte Carlo VaR.

algorithm.variant: quantum risk analysis / QAE for VaR

problem_formulation.encoding_details: Random variable X discretized over M=2^m states |i>; an ancillary qubit is flipped according to indicator function f(i) for i<=k.
problem_formulation.objective_function: Find k such that FX(x<=k) >= alpha; VaR is the corresponding loss threshold.
problem_formulation.constraints_handling: Indicator-function encoding with QAE; no explicit penalty terms.

problem_instance.description: VaR estimation for a portfolio of two assets (China Bao An and Ping An Bank) under a normal distribution model.

dataset_specification.description: Two assets, 10 units of each purchased; 0.95 confidence; 30 holding days.

problem_instance.data_preprocessing_details: Historical returns summarized by mean and variance for P-VaR; Monte Carlo uses geometric Brownian motion; quantum method discretizes the loss distribution.
problem_instance.evaluation_methodology: Results compared across sampling points 1,2,4,...,512; quantum VaR compared to H-VaR, P-VaR, and MC-VaR.

implementation_details.classical_preprocessing: Discretize loss distribution; map threshold index k to ancilla-flip indicator.
implementation_details.classical_postprocessing: Infer VaR from measured ancilla probability and compare against classical baselines.

speedup_claims.conditions: QAE-based VaR estimation; precision scaling O(M^-1) versus MC-VaR O(M^-1/2)
speedup_claims.caveats: The paper gives an asymptotic precision claim, not a runtime benchmark.

speedup_claims.factor: closer to P-VaR than MC-VaR at the same sampling point
speedup_claims.conditions: example with 0.95 confidence, 30 holding days, two assets, sampling points 1 to 512
speedup_claims.caveats: No exact numeric VaR values are provided for each sampling point in the text; only the figure and qualitative comparison are reported.

advantage_assessment.resources_for_advantage: An m-qubit sampled register plus one ancilla are described; no concrete qubit count, depth, or shot budget is reported.
limiting_factors: Only a quadratic precision improvement over Monte Carlo is claimed
No concrete hardware execution details are reported
The example is a small portfolio with two assets and 30 holding days
Classical baselines include H-VaR, P-VaR, and MC-VaR, with the quantum method mainly matching P-VaR at sufficient sampling

notes: Hardware type inferred as real_qpu_superconducting from the paper's statement that BQ-Bank can run on a real superconducting quantum computer; no specific device is named.
The paper describes m sampled qubits plus one ancillary qubit, but does not state a concrete total qubit count for the example.
The paper reports the quantum VaR estimate approaches P-VaR and outperforms MC-VaR in precision, but this is a small illustrative instance rather than a practical advantage demonstration.

experiments.description: QAOA-based portfolio optimization for selecting a subset of assets under a budget and risk-return objective, with a hybrid classical post-optimization step.

algorithm.variant: QAOA for mean-variance combinatorial portfolio optimization
algorithm.convergence_criteria: iterate until the classical optimizer approximately reaches a minimum

hyperparameters.b: investment budget / number of assets to purchase

problem_formulation.encoding_details: Binary decision variable xi indicates whether asset i is purchased; mapped to Pauli-Z via xi -> (I - sigma_z_i)/2.
problem_formulation.objective_function: min_{x in {0,1}^n} q x^T C x - mu^T x subject to 1^T x = b; implemented with penalty Lx = q sum_{i,j} C_{ji} x_i x_j - sum_i mu_i x_i + A(b - sum_i x_i)^2.
problem_formulation.constraints_handling: Penalty term A(b - sum_i x_i)^2; assets with minx > 0 are fixed in advance, reducing the QAOA subproblem.
problem_formulation.problem_hamiltonian: H_C = C(sigma_z^1, ..., sigma_z^n) after mapping xi -> (I - sigma_z_i)/2; mixing Hamiltonian H_B = sum_i sigma_x_i.

problem_instance.description: Portfolio optimization over candidate financial assets with fixed budget and risk-return tradeoff.

dataset_specification.description: Historical period [t_i, t_f] for candidate assets; example shown in figures but asset list not fully enumerated in text.

problem_instance.data_preprocessing_details: Assets with minx > 0 are assigned to a fixed set X1; remaining assets X2 are optimized by QAOA; final proportions are optimized classically with trust-constr.
problem_instance.evaluation_methodology: Single worked example shown in figures; quantum-selected portfolio compared with historical return curve.

implementation_details.classical_solver: COBYLA; trust-constr; classical post-processing for portfolio proportions
implementation_details.classical_preprocessing: Split assets into fixed and variable subsets based on minx; convert binary variables to Ising form.
implementation_details.classical_postprocessing: Use trust-constr to optimize asset proportions after QAOA selects the subset.

speedup_claims.caveats: The paper reports a worked example and a hybrid workflow, but no explicit classical baseline, runtime comparison, approximation ratio, or speedup metric.

advantage_assessment.resources_for_advantage: A QAOA variational circuit with p layers is described, but no qubit count, circuit depth, or hardware execution metrics are reported.
limiting_factors: The method is hybrid and relies on classical optimization (COBYLA and trust-constr)
No benchmark against strong classical combinatorial solvers is reported
No evidence of practical quantum advantage is provided
Problem size and hardware resource usage are not quantified

notes: The paper explicitly describes QAOA and a hybrid classical-quantum workflow, but does not report a concrete qubit count, circuit depth p, or gate counts for the portfolio instance.
Hardware type is inferred as real_qpu_superconducting from the paper's general statement that BQ-Bank can run on a real superconducting quantum computer; no specific device is named.
No asymptotic speedup order is formally derived for the portfolio optimization experiment; the paper only claims better empirical performance in the example.
The paper presents QAOA as a hybrid heuristic for portfolio optimization, but does not demonstrate superiority over classical optimization at scale.
